title: Disk Forensics with Autopsy
description: Students install Autopsy, create a new forensic case using a provided Windows disk image, run automated ingest modules to surface key artifacts, perform timeline analysis to reconstruct attacker activity, recover deleted files, examine browser and registry artifacts, and produce a forensic report with findings and evidence supporting an incident timeline.
objective: Students will use Autopsy to conduct a structured disk forensics investigation on a Windows disk image from a simulated compromise, identify attacker persistence mechanisms, recover deleted payload files, examine browser download history, analyse relevant registry keys, and produce a professional forensic timeline and artifact summary.

steps.title: Install Autopsy and Create a New Forensic Case
steps.instructions:
Download and install Autopsy, then create a properly documented forensic case.

**Download Autopsy:**
- URL: https://www.autopsy.com/download/
- Windows installer (~700 MB, includes Sleuth Kit)
- Minimum requirements: 4 GB RAM, 10 GB free disk

**Launch Autopsy and create a new case:**
1. Open Autopsy → Click **New Case**
2. Enter case details:
   - Case Name: `Lab05-DiskForensics`
   - Base Directory: `C:\ForensicCases\` (create this folder first)
   - Case Number: `INC-2026-005`
   - Examiner: Your name

3. Add a data source — select **Disk Image or VM File**
4. Point to the provided disk image: `windows-compromise.E01` (or `.dd`)
   - Download from course resources portal or use the NIST CFReDS sample:
   - https://www.cfreds.nist.gov/data_leakage_case/data-leakage-case.html

5. On the **Configure Ingest Modules** screen, enable ALL modules for a full automated analysis:
   - Recent Activity
   - Hash Lookup (NSRL database)
   - File Type Identification
   - Keyword Search
   - Interesting Files Identifier
   - Windows Registry
   - Email Parser

6. Click **Finish** and wait for ingest to complete (can take 15-60 minutes depending on image size).

steps.title: Run Timeline Analysis and Identify the Attack Window
steps.instructions:
Use Autopsy's Timeline tool to reconstruct a chronological view of file system activity and identify the timeframe of the attack.

**Open Timeline:**
1. In Autopsy, go to **Tools → Timeline**
2. The timeline viewer opens in a new window
3. Select the **Counts** view first to see overall activity distribution
   - Look for unusual spikes in file creation/modification activity
4. Switch to **Details** view to examine specific events

**Navigate to the suspected compromise timeframe:**
- Use the date range controls to zoom into the attack window
- Look for clusters of activity outside normal business hours

**Filter for high-value event types:**
- File Created (FC) in `C:\Users\`, `C:\Temp\`, `C:\ProgramData\`
- Registry Last Written (RLW) in Run keys
- Web Downloads

**Export the attack window timeline:**
1. File → Export → CSV
2. Open in Excel or LibreOffice
3. Filter for `C:\Users\` paths and sort by timestamp

**Document:** Create a table with the 10 most significant timeline events:
```
| Timestamp (UTC) | Event Type | File/Registry Path | Significance |
```

steps.title: Recover Deleted Files and Analyse Downloads
steps.instructions:
Use Autopsy's file recovery and browser artifact analysis to find evidence of payload delivery.

**Find deleted files:**
1. In the directory tree (left panel), expand the image and navigate to:
   - `vol1 > Users > [username] > AppData > Local > Temp`
   - `vol1 > Users > [username] > Downloads`
   - `vol1 > Windows > Temp`
2. In each folder, look for files marked with a red ❌ icon (deleted)
3. Right-click a deleted file → **Extract File** to recover it

**Recover specific file types using search:**
1. Go to **Tools → File Search by Attributes**
2. Search for extension `.exe` in `C:\Users\`
3. Search for `.ps1` (PowerShell scripts) anywhere
4. Filter by date: within the suspected attack window

**Analyse browser download history:**
1. In the left panel, navigate to **Results → Extracted Content → Web Downloads**
2. Review the list: URL downloaded from, local filename, timestamp
3. Look for:
   - Executables downloaded from unusual domains
   - Tools like `mimikatz`, `whoami`, `nc.exe`, `psexec`
   - Downloads just before suspicious file creation events

**Calculate hashes of recovered files:**
1. Right-click a recovered file → **Extract File(s)**
2. In your working directory, calculate SHA-256:
```powershell
Get-FileHash .\recovered_payload.exe -Algorithm SHA256
```
3. Submit to VirusTotal and document the result.

steps.title: Examine Windows Registry for Persistence Mechanisms
steps.instructions:
Analyse the Windows Registry hives within the disk image to identify persistence mechanisms installed by the attacker.

**Access registry analysis in Autopsy:**
1. In the left panel, go to **Results → Extracted Content → OS Accounts** to see user accounts
2. Go to **Data Artifacts → Recent Documents** for recently opened files
3. Go to **Installed Programs** to see what software was present

**Directly examine registry hives:**
1. Navigate in directory tree to: `vol1 > Windows > System32 > config`
2. You'll find: `SAM`, `SECURITY`, `SOFTWARE`, `SYSTEM`
3. Right-click `SOFTWARE` → **Open in External Viewer** → Open with Registry Viewer
   - Or extract hive to disk and use `RegRipper` or `Registry Explorer`

**Key registry locations to check:**
```
Persistence:
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce
HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Service persistence:
HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\[ServiceName]

Recent activity (user registry - NTUSER.DAT):
HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RecentDocs
HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU
```

**Using RegRipper for batch extraction:**
```bash
rip.exe -r SOFTWARE -f software > software_report.txt
rip.exe -r NTUSER.DAT -f ntuser > ntuser_report.txt
grep -i "run\|startup\|service" software_report.txt
```

**Document any run key entries that reference unusual executable paths** — these are persistence IOCs.

steps.title: Write a Forensic Timeline and Submit Evidence
steps.instructions:
Compile all findings into a professional forensic artifact report with a complete evidence timeline.

**Create your forensic report using this structure:**

```
====================================================
FORENSIC ANALYSIS REPORT
====================================================
Case:        Lab05-DiskForensics / INC-2026-005
Examiner:    [Your Name]
Date:        [Today's Date]
Disk Image:  windows-compromise.E01
Hash (SHA256): [image hash from acquisition]

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
[2-3 sentences: what happened, when, key findings]

ARTIFACT TIMELINE
-----------------
[Date/Time UTC] | [Artifact Type] | [Path/Value] | [Significance]
...

DELETED FILES RECOVERED
-----------------------
Filename:    payload.exe
Original path: C:\Users\victim\AppData\Local\Temp\payload.exe
SHA256:      [hash]
VT Result:  45/72 detections (Cobalt Strike Beacon)

BROWSER ARTIFACTS
-----------------
Download URL:  http://evil-host[.]com/payload.exe
Downloaded:    [timestamp]
Browser:       Chrome (version X)

REGISTRY PERSISTENCE
--------------------
Key:    HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
Value:  WindowsUpdate
Data:   C:\ProgramData\update.exe

IOC SUMMARY
-----------
Filename:  payload.exe, update.exe
Hashes:    [SHA256 values]
Domain:    evil-host[.]com
Path:      C:\ProgramData\update.exe

ATT&CK MAPPING
--------------
T1105  - Ingress Tool Transfer (payload downloaded via browser)
T1547.001 - Registry Run Keys (HKLM Run persistence)
T1003.001 - OS Credential Dumping (mimikatz strings found)
====================================================
```

**Final steps:**
1. Export the Autopsy case as a report: **Generate Report → HTML Report**
2. Take screenshots of: deleted files view, browser downloads, registry run key
3. Create a SHA-256 hash list of all recovered evidence files
4. Package everything into: `lab05b-[yourname].zip`

expected_output: Students submit: (1) Autopsy HTML report exported from the case, (2) screenshot of Timeline Analysis showing activity spike during attack window, (3) at least one recovered deleted file with its SHA-256 hash and VirusTotal result, (4) screenshot of browser download history showing malicious payload URL, (5) screenshot of registry Run key showing persistence entry, (6) completed forensic report in the provided template format.
